story.title: Huawei Convicted of Trade Secrets Theft, Acquitted of Racketeering Charges
story.summary: A federal jury in Brooklyn found Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts related to stealing trade secrets and deceiving banks about its business in Iran. However, the company was acquitted of the more serious charge of engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The verdict concludes a months-long trial.

explore_lenses.label: Why does the verdict matter beyond this case?
explore_lenses.title: It reinforces an already restrictive U.S. posture
explore_lenses.summary: The convictions add criminal findings to a years-long U.S. campaign that has already limited Huawei’s access to U.S. technology and telecom markets. The racketeering acquittal narrows the government’s courtroom win, but does not erase the convictions on the remaining counts.

claims.text: Huawei and specified affiliates were placed on the Commerce Department’s Entity List in May 2019, creating licensing requirements for exports, reexports and in-country transfers of items subject to U.S. export controls.

The FCC’s Covered List, updated in May 2026, identifies Huawei telecommunications and video-surveillance equipment and services as covered equipment or services; Huawei was included on March 12, 2021.

The jury’s acquittal on racketeering means it did not find Huawei guilty of the government’s overarching allegation that the company operated as a criminal enterprise, even while convicting it on 10 other counts.

explore_lenses.label: How did the case reach a 2026 verdict?
explore_lenses.title: A 2019 case expanded into a broad corporate prosecution
explore_lenses.summary: The prosecution grew from allegations about Iran-related banking disclosures and T-Mobile trade secrets into a 2020 superseding indictment alleging a long-running pattern involving multiple Huawei entities. The jury trial began after years of pretrial litigation.

claims.text: The Justice Department’s January 2019 indictment alleged that Huawei used Skycom, described by prosecutors as an unofficial Iran-based subsidiary, while misrepresenting the Huawei-Skycom relationship to financial institutions.

In February 2020, prosecutors added racketeering and trade-secret-conspiracy counts; the DOJ said the trade-secret allegation concerned an asserted long-running practice of using fraud and deception to obtain U.S. companies’ technology.

A 2026 court filing alleged conduct involving several victim companies from 2000 through 2020, including confidential technical information and a 2013 incident involving a T-Mobile testing robot; these were prosecution allegations, not separate findings described in the verdict report.
Huawei’s defense argued that prosecutors had turned isolated employee conduct and material it said was public into a false company-wide conspiracy narrative.

explore_lenses.label: What happens next for Huawei?
explore_lenses.title: Appeal and financial penalties are the next legal issues
explore_lenses.summary: Huawei has said it will appeal the convictions. The remaining proceedings will determine the sentence and any financial consequences, while the company will likely argue that the racketeering acquittal undercuts the government’s broader narrative.

claims.text: Huawei attorney Brian Heberlig said after the verdict that the company would appeal the convictions and characterized the racketeering acquittal as a rejection of the government’s central narrative.
The 2020 superseding indictment gave notice that the government would seek criminal forfeiture upon convictions on multiple counts, including property or proceeds connected to the offenses.

Forecast: the appeal will focus on alleged legal or evidentiary errors and could delay finality; that expectation follows from Huawei’s announced intent to appeal, but no appellate filing or schedule had been identified in the reporting consulted.

story_report.summary: A jury convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 criminal counts involving trade-secret theft and deception of banks, while acquitting the company of racketeering charges. The split verdict leaves Huawei guilty on the counts of conviction but rejects the government’s overarching criminal-enterprise allegation. Huawei attorney Brian Heberlig said the company will appeal, meaning the convictions are likely to face further court review before the case is final.

sections.heading: Huawei Case Included Iran Allegations
sections.body: The Justice Department’s 2019 indictment alleged that Huawei used Skycom, which prosecutors described as an unofficial Iran-based subsidiary, while misrepresenting the relationship between the companies to financial institutions. Prosecutors added racketeering and trade-secret-conspiracy counts in 2020, alleging a long-running practice of using fraud and deception to obtain U.S. companies’ technology. A later court filing described alleged conduct involving several companies between 2000 and 2020, including confidential technical information and a 2013 incident involving a T-Mobile testing robot; those allegations were not separate verdict findings.

sections.heading: Huawei Defense Challenged Government Narrative
sections.body: Huawei’s defense argued that prosecutors had treated isolated employee conduct and material the company considered public as evidence of a false company-wide conspiracy. After the verdict, Heberlig characterized the racketeering acquittal as a rejection of the government’s central narrative. The announced appeal is expected to focus on claimed legal or evidentiary errors, although no appellate filing or schedule had been identified in the reporting consulted.

sections.heading: Huawei Remains Subject to US Restrictions
sections.body: The verdict does not itself establish new U.S. restrictions, but Huawei already faces significant federal limits. Huawei and specified affiliates were added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List in May 2019, imposing licensing requirements for certain exports, reexports and in-country transfers. The FCC’s Covered List also identifies Huawei telecommunications and video-surveillance equipment and services as covered, with Huawei included in March 2021.

unresolved.text: The sentencing date, any fine or forfeiture amount, the specific appellate arguments, and whether the verdict will prompt further U.S. restrictions have not been established.
The immediate effect of the verdict on Huawei’s overseas business and future U.S. regulatory decisions remains unclear.

related_stories.title: Huawei Found Guilty of Conspiracy to Steal Trade Secrets and Bank Fraud
related_stories.summary: A U.S. jury has convicted Huawei Technologies of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud. The company was accused of stealing technology from U.S. firms, violating U.S. sanctions by doing business with countries like Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to government officials and banks. This conviction represents a significant legal challenge for the Chinese tech giant.

related_stories.summary: China has announced the crew for its upcoming Shenzhou-24 mission, which includes Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a Pakistani astronaut. Ali will be the first foreigner to board China's Tiangong space station. The mission is set to launch on Wednesday.
